specPoints.text: draw magnetic field patterns for a straight wire, a flat circular coil and a solenoid when each is carrying a current

primer.text: Three current geometries, three drawable fields: circles around a straight wire, a strong axial line through a flat coil, and a bar-magnet twin with a uniform core inside a solenoid. This note is a drawing course — cross and dot conventions, grip-rule polarities, and the spacing that shows strength.

lessons.title: Drawing the field of a straight wire
sourceHeadings: Magnetic field in a straight wire
lessons.opening: A current-carrying straight wire draws its own field: circles around the wire, clockwise or anticlockwise depending on the current direction, given by the right-hand grip. The drawing skill is to show the circles in the plane perpendicular to the wire, with the current marked into or out of the page.
keyPoints: The field pattern for a straight wire is circles centred on the wire.
The circle direction follows the current by the right-hand grip rule.
Current into the page is drawn with a cross; current out with a dot.
The circles are drawn closest together near the wire where the field is strongest.
The pattern lies in the plane perpendicular to the wire.

low.restatement: Look down the wire: the field circles it like ring after ring. Thumb along the current and the fingers curl the way the rings run.
low.analogy: The rings are like ripples spreading round a pole stuck in water — going all the way round, fading as they spread.
low.examPointer: Use the cross/dot convention and label it — an unlabelled diagram scores half at best.

medium.restatement: The drawn pattern encodes the azimuthal field: concentric circles with spacing growing with radius to show the strength falloff. The cross/dot notation projects the axial current onto the page, and the grip rule converts that projection into a definite circulation sense for the drawn circles.
medium.analogy: The diagram is a map viewed from above: the cross or dot is the tunnel under the map, and the circles are the roads looping round it.
medium.examPointer: Drawing marks: concentric, circular, spacing widening outward, plus a labelled current symbol — all four or expect deduction.

check.stem: What shape are the drawn field lines around a straight current-carrying wire?

options.explanation: The straight-wire pattern is concentric circles.

options.text: lines from end to end of the wire
options.explanation: End-to-end lines belong to bar magnets.
Parallel lines are the uniform-gap pattern.
The circles close on themselves; they do not spiral in.

check.stem: A cross is drawn on the wire symbol in a field diagram. It means the current flows:

options.explanation: The cross is the tail feathers of an arrow going away.
Out is drawn as a dot, the arrow tip.

options.text: along the page to the right
options.explanation: In-page directions are drawn as arrows, not crosses.
The cross marks a current, not its absence.

check.stem: How does the drawing show that the field weakens with distance from the wire?

options.text: the circles are spaced further apart with distance
options.explanation: Wider spacing encodes weaker field.

options.text: the circles get smaller with distance
options.explanation: Circles get LARGER with radius; spacing is the cue.
Shape never changes — only spacing.
Spacing is exactly the strength encoding.

check.stem: A student draws the straight-wire pattern with the circles running the wrong way. Which check catches the error?

options.text: applying the right-hand grip rule with the thumb along the current
options.explanation: The grip rule fixes the circulation sense.

options.text: measuring the wire with a ruler
options.explanation: Wire length is unrelated to the circulation sense.
Circle count is a drawing choice, not a physics check.
Mass has no bearing on the field pattern.

check.stem: Which diagram element is ESSENTIAL when drawing the straight-wire pattern?

options.text: the current direction marked with a cross or dot
options.explanation: Without the current label the circulation sense is undefined.
Circle count is a choice, not a requirement.
Colour carries no field meaning here.
The pattern of one wire stands alone.

check.stem: State the shape and direction rule for the field pattern of a straight wire.
check.modelAnswer: Circles centred on the wire, with the circulation direction given by the right-hand grip rule.

check.stem: State the drawing convention for current into and out of the page.
check.modelAnswer: A cross marks current into the page and a dot marks current out of the page.

check.stem: Explain why the drawn circles are closest together right next to the wire.
check.modelAnswer: Line spacing encodes field strength, and the field around a straight wire is strongest at the wire surface and weakens with distance. Drawing the circles crowded at the wire and increasingly spaced outward makes the strength falloff visible in the pattern itself.

check.stem: Sketch-check: a wire carries current out of the page. State the circulation sense of the field circles as seen looking at the page, and name the rule used.
check.modelAnswer: With the dot showing current towards the viewer, the grip rule gives anticlockwise circles as seen on the page — thumb pointing out at you, fingers curling anticlockwise. The rule used is the right-hand grip rule.

lessons.title: The flat circular coil's field
sourceHeadings: Magnetic field in a flat circular coil
lessons.opening: Bend the wire into a flat circular coil and every turn contributes its circles: through the centre of the coil all the contributions point the same way, so the field there is strong and axial. The drawn pattern shows crowded, nearly straight lines through the coil's middle, fanning out on either side.
keyPoints: Each turn of a flat circular coil adds its own circular field.
At the coil's centre all turns give field in the same axial direction.
The field at the centre is stronger than one wire's field alone.
The drawn pattern is nearly straight through the centre, curling round outside.
More turns or more current strengthens the coil's central field.

low.restatement: One loop of wire makes circles; stack the loop's effect with every extra turn and the middle of the coil gets a strong, straight-through field.
low.analogy: One person clapping is quiet; a ring of people clapping in step is loud — the centre of the ring hears them all at once.
low.examPointer: Say the contributions 'add' or 'reinforce' at the centre — 'each turn helps' scores nothing without the adding.

medium.restatement: At the geometric centre every turn's azimuthal field points along the same axis, so the superposition is maximal there; the drawn axial lines are straight and crowded, bending round to close outside the coil. Strength scales with the number of turns and the current per turn, which is why the coil is half-way to a solenoid.
medium.analogy: Each turn is one lens focusing the field onto the central axis; more lenses, tighter focus, brighter line.
medium.examPointer: Contrast with the single wire: same current, but the coil's centre field is many times stronger because every turn contributes.

check.stem: Why is the field at the centre of a flat coil stronger than one wire's field?

options.text: every turn contributes field in the same direction there
options.explanation: The contributions add at the centre.

options.text: the coil stores charge at the centre
options.explanation: No charge accumulates; fields add, not charge.

options.text: the coil's wire is thicker at the centre
options.explanation: Wire thickness is uniform around the coil.

options.text: the centre is closer to the battery
options.explanation: Distance to the battery is irrelevant to the pattern.

check.stem: How are the field lines drawn through the CENTRE of a flat circular coil?

options.text: nearly straight along the axis, crowded together
options.explanation: The centre field is strong and axial.
The central field has one clear direction.
Field lines never cross.

options.text: absent — the centre has no field
options.explanation: The centre has the STRONGEST field.

check.stem: Doubling the number of turns on a flat coil, keeping the current the same, does what to the central field?

options.explanation: More turns, more contributing fields.
More turns add, not subtract.
Direction follows the current sense, unchanged here.
Turn count is a strength factor.

check.stem: The current in a flat coil is reversed. What happens to the drawn pattern?

options.text: the pattern is mirrored — every field direction reverses
options.explanation: The axial field flips to the other direction.
Arrows all reverse with the current.

options.text: the pattern becomes a straight-wire pattern
options.explanation: Shape follows geometry, not current sense.
The contributions still add — in the new direction.

check.stem: Which statement about a single turn and a many-turn coil of the same radius and current is correct?

options.text: the many-turn coil has the stronger central field
options.explanation: Turns stack the same-direction contributions.

options.text: the single turn has the stronger central field
options.explanation: Fewer contributions means a weaker total.
Turn count changes the sum.
Both do — one weakly, one strongly.

check.stem: State why the field lines through the coil centre point in one common direction.
check.modelAnswer: Each turn of the coil gives a field contribution in the same axial direction at the centre, so they add to one common direction.

check.stem: State two ways to strengthen the central field of a flat coil.
check.modelAnswer: Add more turns to the coil or increase the current through it.

check.stem: Explain why the drawn pattern of a flat coil looks like a bar magnet's field rather than a straight wire's.
check.modelAnswer: The stacked turns give the coil two effective faces — field leaving one side and entering the other — like the poles of a bar magnet, so the external lines curl from face to face. A straight wire has no such faces: its field is pure circles with no pole structure to draw.

check.stem: A flat coil of 40 turns carries 2 A; a second coil of 80 turns carries 1 A at the same radius. Compare the two central fields and justify the comparison.
check.modelAnswer: The central field scales with turns times current, so the first coil gives 40 × 2 = 80 units and the second 80 × 1 = 80 units — the two central fields are equal in strength and point along the same axial geometry determined by each coil's winding sense.

lessons.title: The solenoid's field and its strength levers
sourceHeadings: Factors affecting magnetic field strength of a solenoid
lessons.opening: A solenoid is a long coil, and its field is the bar magnet's field reborn: outside, lines curl from a north end to a south end; inside, they run straight, parallel and crowded. The right-hand grip rule adapted to the whole coil names the poles, and turns, current and a soft iron core set the strength.
keyPoints: A solenoid is a long coil of wire carrying a current.
Outside, its field pattern matches a bar magnet's, with poles at the ends.
Inside, the field is strong, straight and parallel along the axis.
The right-hand grip rule on the coil gives the north end.
More turns, a larger current and a soft iron core each strengthen the field.

low.restatement: Curl the wire into a spring shape and switch on: one end acts north, the other south, and the field inside runs straight down the tube. Fingers curl with the wire's current; the thumb points to the north end.
low.analogy: The solenoid is a magnet you can dial up: twist the current knob and the invisible bar magnet inside gets stronger or weaker.
low.examPointer: Inside-solenoid lines are 'straight and parallel' — that phrase signals uniformity and earns the pattern mark.

medium.restatement: Each turn's contribution adds along the shared axis, so the interior superposes into a near-uniform axial field while the exterior closes the loops like a bar magnet's. The adapted grip rule reads the wrapped current to name the poles; strength scales with turns per length, current, and the induced soft iron core that multiplies the interior field.
medium.analogy: A solenoid is a ladder of coil-turns: every rung adds the same axial push, and the iron core turns the ladder into an escalator.
medium.examPointer: Polarity questions: curl the RIGHT hand's fingers with the current around the coil — the thumb gives the north-seeking end. Left hand gives the wrong pole.

check.stem: The field pattern OUTSIDE a current-carrying solenoid resembles:

options.text: the field of a bar magnet
options.explanation: The external pattern runs pole to pole like a magnet's.
That is the single-wire pattern, not a solenoid's.
The solenoid has a full external field.
The uniform-gap pattern is inside, not outside.

check.stem: The field lines INSIDE a solenoid are drawn:

options.text: straight, parallel and crowded along the axis
options.explanation: The interior field is strong and uniform.
The turns' circles add into the axial field inside.
Field lines never cross.
Radiation is not the solenoid's interior pattern.

check.stem: Which rule names the poles of a solenoid?

options.text: the right-hand grip rule applied to the coil
options.explanation: Curl with the current; the thumb gives the north end.
That rule predicts forces, not solenoid polarity.
A gas law has no role here.

options.text: trial and error with iron filings only
options.explanation: Filings show the pattern; the grip rule names the poles.

check.stem: A soft iron core is slid inside a current-carrying solenoid. What happens?

options.text: the interior field becomes much stronger
options.explanation: The induced core multiplies the field.
Induction strengthens, never weakens, the applied field.
Core insertion changes strength, not polarity.
The axial pattern is preserved and strengthened.

check.stem: Which THREE changes all strengthen a solenoid's field?

options.text: more turns, larger current, soft iron core
options.explanation: These are the three strength levers.

options.text: fewer turns, larger current, plastic core
options.explanation: Fewer turns weakens; plastic is non-magnetic.

options.text: more turns, smaller current, steel core left permanent
options.explanation: Smaller current weakens; permanent steel defeats the switch-off.

options.text: longer wire everywhere but same turns and current
options.explanation: Extra length alone adds nothing to the field.

check.stem: State what a solenoid is.
check.modelAnswer: A solenoid is a long coil of wire that carries a current and acts like a bar magnet.

check.stem: State how the right-hand grip rule names the poles of a solenoid.
check.modelAnswer: Curl the fingers of the right hand with the current around the coil; the thumb points to the north end.

check.stem: Explain why the interior field of a solenoid is strong and uniform.
check.modelAnswer: Every turn adds a field contribution in the same axial direction inside the coil, so the contributions stack into a large total. Because the turns are evenly wound, the sum is the same at every interior point along the middle, giving a straight, parallel, equally spaced pattern — a uniform field.

check.stem: An electromagnet crane uses a solenoid with 200 turns at 4 A on a soft iron core. State two independent upgrades for a stronger lift and one reason a permanent steel core would be a mistake.
check.modelAnswer: Upgrade the current above 4 A, or add turns above 200 — either lever strengthens the field for a stronger lift. A permanent steel core is a mistake because it would keep holding the scrap after switch-off: the crane could lift but never release.

glossary.definition: Wire wound into a flat loop whose turns add their fields at the centre.
A long coil of wire whose field matches a bar magnet's, with a strong uniform interior field.
Cross for current into the page, dot for current out of the page.
